problem.text:
Consider a grid of points where each point is coloured either white or black, such that no two rows have the same sequence of colours and no two columns have the same sequence of colours. Let a table denote four points on the grid that form the vertices of a rectangle with sides parallel to those of the grid. A table is called balanced if one diagonal pair of points are coloured white and the other diagonal pair black.
Determine all possible values of $k \geq 2$ for which there exists a colouring of a $k \times 2019$ grid with no balanced tables.

cues.why_it_matters: Write white as $0$ and black as $1$ ($0$ is white, $1$ is black). Then a table is balanced exactly when one diagonal has $0$ at both ends and the other diagonal has $1$ at both ends, for example $0$ at top-left and bottom-right and $1$ at the other two corners.
cues.how_spotted: Copy the diagonal description into a $2$ by $2$ box and fill the two diagonals with opposite colours.

cues.why_it_matters: The ban applies to every table in the $k \times 2019$ grid, so it can be read on just two rows at a time: pick two rows and look at what pairs appear down the $2019$ columns.
cues.how_spotted: Underline no and ask what choice of two rows and two columns would break it.

cues.why_it_matters: For $k \geq 2$ the answer needs both directions: one colouring with distinct rows, distinct columns and no balanced table for each good $k$, and a reason no other $k$ works.
cues.how_spotted: Split determine all into two jobs: build one example where possible and rule out where impossible.

cues.why_it_matters: Only one $k \times 2019$ colouring with distinct rows, distinct columns and no balanced table is needed per $k$, so a staircase, meaning rows like $100$, $110$, $111$ that add $1$s step by step, can certify its $k$ in the $k \times 2019$ grid even if most colourings fail. Keep $3$ columns only as a trial.

goal.asked: What is asked is which heights $k \geq 2$ admit a colouring of the $k \times 2019$ grid with distinct rows, distinct columns and no balanced table.
goal.answer_form: A complete answer gives a list of good heights, each with one explicit colouring with distinct rows, distinct columns and no balanced table, plus a proof that no other height admits such a colouring.
goal.final_line_would_say: The final line would say the good heights are exactly those listed, each with its example and with all other heights ruled out.

deeper_properties: A table is fixed by two distinct rows and two distinct columns, and swapping the two columns does not change whether it is balanced.
Distinctness of rows and columns is about whole strings of length $2019$ or $k$, so two rows can agree in many places and still be distinct.

candidates.name: Binary rows ordered pointwise
candidates.from_first_principles: A balanced table on two rows $x$, $y$ is both $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$ appearing down the $2019$ columns, so banning it misses one mixed pair for each pair of rows. That leaves $x[c]<=y[c]$ for every column $c$ or $y[c]<=x[c]$ for every column $c$. Then distinct rows ordered this way nest strictly while each column down the rows is $0^t1^{k-t}$ with $t$ the count of $0$s, and counting these row and column possibilities squeezes $k$ from both sides and points to staircase colourings.
candidates.why: It uses every lever: the diagonal pattern gives the two mixed column types, the global ban lines rows up, and distinct rows and columns turn the lining-up into a count with matching staircase examples.

candidates.name: Count whole rows and columns alone
candidates.from_first_principles: Distinct rows and distinct columns look like a counting problem about binary strings, so count them directly.
candidates.why: Counting strings alone ignores the ban on balanced tables, which is the only link between a pair of rows and a pair of columns.

candidates.name: Build freely for many rows
candidates.from_first_principles: Since only one colouring per $k$ is needed, try to extend examples to arbitrarily many rows while keeping columns distinct.
candidates.why: Two rows that disagree in both directions already make a balanced table, so free extension keeps hitting the forbidden diagonal pattern.

method.chosen: Binary rows ordered pointwise; rows form a chain, counted by nested sets and column shapes, with staircase examples.
